text: Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 1 BIG DATA UNIT-3 Pig: Comparison with Databases, Pig Latin -Structure, Statements, Expressions, Types, Schemas, Functions, Macros, User -Defined Functions- A Filter UDF, An Eval UDF, A Load UDF; Data Processing Operators- Loading and Storing Data, Filtering Data, Grouping and Joi ning Data, Sorting Data, Combining and Splitting Data, Pig in Practice Parallelism, Anonymous Relations, Parameter Substitution Flume: working with flume, Transactions and Reliability, The HDFS Sink, Fan Out, Distribution --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Pig Overview and Pig Latin 1. Comparison with Databases: o Pig is a high-level platform for creating MapReduce programs used with Hadoop. o Unlike traditional databases, Pig is optimized for batch processing large datasets. o Pig provides a scripting interface (Pig Latin) rather than SQL queries. 2. Pig Latin: o Structure: Series of statements forming a data flow. o Statements: Assign data to variables, perform operations. o Expressions: Used to transform or compute data. o Types: Basic types include int, long, float, double, chararray, bytearray, and bag.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 2 o Schemas: Define the structure of data with field names and types. o Functions: Built-in and user-defined functions (UDFs) for data manipulation. o Macros: Reusable blocks of Pig Latin code. o User-Defined Functions (UDFs): ▪ Filter UDF: Filters tuples based on a condition. ▪ Eval UDF: Computes new values from input. ▪ Load UDF: Custom load functions to ingest data. 3. Data Processing Operators: o Loading and Storing Data: LOAD and STORE commands for reading and writing datasets. o Filtering Data: FILTER operator to select tuples based on conditions. o Grouping and Joining Data: GROUP, COGROUP, and JOIN operators to organize and combine data. o Sorting Data: ORDER operator to sort datasets. o Combining and Splitting Data: UNION to combine, SPLIT to divide datasets. 4. Pig in Practice: o Parallelism: Control parallel execution of operations for performance. Parallelism: Control with PARALLEL keyword. Example: GROUP data BY dept PARALLEL 5; o Anonymous Relations: Temporary relations not stored in variables. Anonymous Relations: Intermediate results without alias. Example: DUMP (FILTER (LOAD 'data') BY age>18); o Parameter Substitution: Pass parameters at runtime to Pig scripts for dynamic behavior.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 3 o Parser: The Parser is responsible for accepting Pig scripts and doing the necessary validations for the script . It first checks whether the script is syntactically correct or not, and if there is any syntax error in the script then it immediately throws an error. o Optimizer: The Optimizer optimizes the Pig Latin script by performing different optimizations, such as reducing the number of MapReduce jobs and optimizing the execution plan. The optimizer takes the AST generated by the Parser and produces a logical plan. o Compiler: In the compiler phase, the complication of the optimized logical plan is done into small Mapreduce jobs and passed to the execution engine. o The Execution Engine translates the optimized Pig Latin script into a

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 4 series of MapReduce jobs and orchestrates their execution on a Hadoop cluster. It essentially acts as the bridge between Pig's high -level language and Hadoop's distributed processing capabilities Role: The Execution Engine is responsible for the actual data processing within Pig. Function: It takes the optimized Pig Latin script (logical plan) and converts it into a physical plan, which is a series of MapReduce jobs. MapReduce Jobs: These MapReduce jobs are then submitted to the Hadoop cluster for execution. Interaction with Hadoop: The Exe cution Engine interacts with Hadoop's YARN, HDFS, and MapReduce layers to process Pig scripts, translating them into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of MapReduce jobs for efficient execution. Execution Modes: Pig scripts can be executed in different modes, including: Grunt Shell (Interactive mode): Allows users to interactively write and execute Pig Latin scripts. Script Mode (Batch mode): Allows users to run Pig scripts from a file. Embedded Mode: Allows users to embed Pig execution within Java applications. Local Mode: Pig can also be run in local mode, where the data and Pig scripts are

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 5 processed on a single machine. Components: The Execution Engine typically has two main components: Pig Latin Compiler: Compiles the Pig Latin script into a logical plan. Pig Latin Runtime: Executes the logical plan on the Hadoop cluster. Parameter Substitution: Pass parameters to scripts. Example: Script: $input replaced at runtime. Run: pig -param input='data.txt' script.pig Pig: Comparison with Databases Aspect Apache Pig Databases (RDBMS) Purpose Large-scale data analysis on Hadoop. Transactional & operational data management. Data Model Bags, tuples, and fields (semi-structured). Tables with rows and columns (structured). Language Pig Latin (procedural). SQL (declarative). Schema Optional. Mandatory. Data Size Huge datasets (TBs/PBs). Smaller to medium datasets. Execution Compiled into MapReduce/Tez/Spark jobs. Executes via DB query engine.
Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 6 Fault Tolerance Inherits Hadoop’s fault tolerance. Relies on DB backup/recovery systems.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 7 Pig Latin – Structure Pig Latin is a high -level scripting language designed to process large -scale datasets on Hadoop. Its structure is based on a data flow model, where the output of one operation is fed as input into the next. This approach allows developers to build modular, readable, and maintainable scripts. A Pig Latin script generally follows: 1. Load Data – from HDFS or local. 2. Transform Data – filtering, grouping, joining, etc. 3. Store/Display Results – write back to HDFS or output. Relations: • Collections of tuples, similar to tables in a database. • Every operation produces a new relation that can be used in subsequent operations. 1. Operators • Key operators include: o LOAD: Read data into Pig. o STORE: Write data to storage. o FILTER: Select tuples based on conditions. o GROUP/COGROUP: Organize tuples for aggregation. o JOIN: Combine tuples from multiple relations. o ORDER: Sort tuples. o UNION: Merge multiple relations. o SPLIT: Divide a relation into multiple subsets. o FOREACH...GENERATE: Transform tuples by applying expressions or functions.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 8 2. Statements Statements in Pig Latin are the building blocks of a Pig script. Each statement performs a specific operation on data and contributes to the overall data flow. Understanding statements is critical for writing effective and modular Pig scripts. 1. Purpose of Statements: • Execute data operations such as loading, filtering, transforming, aggregating, or storing data. • Assign intermediate results to relations for subsequent operations. • Define the logical flow of data processing in a script. 2. Types of Statements: • LOAD Statement: o Reads data from external storage into Pig. o Syntax: relation = LOAD 'path' USING loader AS schema; o Example: users = LOAD 'users.txt' USING PigStorage(',') AS (id:int, name:chararray, age:int); • STORE Statement: o Writes processed data to external storage. o Syntax: STORE relation INTO 'path' USING storage_function; o Example: STORE adults INTO 'adults.txt' USING PigStorage(','); • FOREACH...GENERATE Statement: o Transforms data by applying expressions or functions to each tuple. o Example: B = FOREACH A GENERATE name, age + 1; • FILTER Statement: o Selects tuples that satisfy a specified condition. o Example: adults = FILTER users BY age >= 18; • GROUP and COGROUP Statements: o Organize tuples for aggregation or joining.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 9 o Example: grouped = GROUP orders BY customer_id; o COGROUP allows grouping across multiple relations. • JOIN Statement: o Combines tuples from multiple relations based on a common key. o Example: combined = JOIN users BY id, orders BY user_id; • ORDER Statement: o Sorts tuples based on one or more fields. o Example: sorted = ORDER users BY age DESC; • UNION Statement: o Merges multiple relations into one. o Example: all_users = UNION users1, users2; • SPLIT Statement: o Divides a relation into multiple relations based on conditions. o Example: SPLIT users INTO adults IF age >= 18, minors IF age < 18; 3. Best Practices: • Assign each operation to a relation to maintain clear data flow. • Use descriptive names for relations to enhance readability. • Keep statements modular and logically sequenced. • Validate statements against the schema to prevent type mismatches. 3. Expressions Expressions in Pig Latin are used to transform, compute, and manipulate data within Pig scripts. They are essential for data processing operations and can be applied in statements like FOREACH...GENERATE, FILTER, and GROUP. 1. Purpose of Expressions: • Compute new values based on existing data.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 10 • Apply arithmetic, string, logical, or built-in function operations. • Transform data for further processing or analysis. 2. Types of Expressions: • Arithmetic Expressions: Perform calculations on numeric fields. o Operators: +, -, *, /, % o Example: B = FOREACH A GENERATE price * quantity AS total_cost; • String Expressions: Manipulate textual data. o Functions: CONCAT(), SUBSTRING(), UPPER(), LOWER(), TRIM() o Example: names_upper = FOREACH A GENERATE UPPER(name); • Logical Expressions: Evaluate conditions for filtering or conditional processing. o Operators: AND, OR, NOT, ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= o Example: adults = FILTER A BY age >= 18 AND city == 'Delhi'; • Built-in Function Expressions: Use Pig’s built-in functions to compute or aggregate values. o Example: avg_salary = FOREACH dept GENERATE AVG(salary); • Conditional Expressions: Use ternary-like operations to compute values based on conditions. o Example: B = FOREACH A GENERATE (age >= 18 ? 'Adult' : 'Minor') AS age_group; 3. Nesting Expressions: • Expressions can be nested to perform complex transformations. • Example: B = FOREACH A GENERATE UPPER(CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)); 4. Usage in Pig Statements: • FOREACH...GENERATE: Apply expressions to transform or compute new fields.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 11 • FILTER: Use logical expressions to select tuples meeting specific conditions. • GROUP and JOIN: Expressions can define keys or conditions for aggregation and combination. 5. Best Practices: • Keep expressions simple and readable; break complex expressions into multiple steps if necessary. • Use descriptive aliases for computed fields. • Validate expressions against schema to avoid type errors. • Combine expressions with UDFs for reusable, custom computations. Expressions are fundamental in Pig Latin, allowing flexible and powerful data manipulation, computation, and transformation across large-scale datasets. 4. Data Types Pig Latin supports a variety of data types to handle both simple and complex data structures. Understanding these types is essential for effective data processing and transformation. 1. Primitive Data Types: • int: 32-bit signed integer values. • long: 64-bit signed integer values. • float: Single-precision floating-point numbers. • double: Double-precision floating-point numbers. • chararray: String data type used for text. • bytearray: Raw binary data; used when type is unknown or for custom parsing.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 12 2. Complex Data Types: • Tuple: Ordered set of fields, similar to a row in a table. Can contain different data types. o Example: (id:int, name:chararray, age:int) • Bag: Collection of tuples, useful for representing nested or repeated data. o Example: {(name:chararray, quantity:int), (name:chararray, quantity:int)} • Map: Collection of key-value pairs where keys are strings and values can be any type. o Example: ["name"#"John", "age"#30] 3. Usage of Data Types: • Primitive types are used for simple data processing and arithmetic. • Complex types allow representation of hierarchical or nested data, enabling operations on grouped or repeated fields. • Example: orders = LOAD 'orders.txt' AS (order_id:int, items:bag{t:tuple(name:chararray, quantity:int)}); 4. Type Casting: • Pig supports explicit type casting to convert between types. • Syntax: (type) expression • Example: B = FOREACH A GENERATE (int)age; 5. Benefits of Understanding Data Types: • Ensure data correctness and consistency. • Enable appropriate operations (e.g., arithmetic on numeric types, string manipulation on chararray). • Improve performance by avoiding unnecessary type conversions.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 13 6. Best Practices: • Always define schemas with correct data types when loading data. • Use complex types like tuple, bag, and map only when necessary to represent hierarchical data. • Validate input data to match expected types to prevent runtime errors. 5. Schemas Schemas in Pig Latin define the structure of the data, including field names and their corresponding data types. While Pig is schema -less by default, specifying schemas provides clarity, improves error checking, and facilitates complex data processing. 1. Purpose of Schemas: • Assign meaningful field names to data columns. • Define data types for fields to enable validation and type checking. • Improve readability and maintainability of Pig scripts. • Facilitate integration with other tools that expect structured data. 2. Syntax for Defining Schemas: • Schemas can be specified when loading data using the AS keyword. • Example: users = LOAD 'users.txt' USING PigStorage(',') AS (id:int, name:chararray, age:int, city:chararray); • Here, each field has a name and a type: id is an integer, name and city are strings, and age is an integer.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 14 3. Supported Data Types: • Primitive types: int, long, float, double, chararray, bytearray • Complex types: tuple, bag, map • Example of complex types: orders = LOAD 'orders.txt' AS (order_id:int, items:bag{t:tuple(name:chararray, quantity:int)}); 4. Using Schemas with Operations: • Schemas help in SELECT, FILTER, GROUP, JOIN, and FOREACH...GENERATE operations. • They allow field referencing by name rather than position, reducing errors. • Example: adults = FILTER users BY age >= 18; names = FOREACH adults GENERATE name, city; 5. Benefits of Using Schemas: • Error Detection: Catch type mismatches or missing fields early. • Readability: Scripts become easier to understand. • Maintainability: Easier to modify and extend scripts. • Integration: Facilitates interaction with relational systems, HBase, and analytics tools. 6. Best Practices: • Always define schemas for clarity, especially for large or complex datasets. • Use descriptive field names that convey the meaning of data. • When using complex types, clearly document nested structures.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 15 By using schemas, Pig Latin scripts gain structure, readability, and robustness, enabling efficient and error-free processing of large-scale data. 6. Functions Functions in Pig Latin are used to perform operations on data within a Pig script. They are a key componen t that enables transformation, computation, and aggregation of data. Pig provides a rich set of built-in functions and also allows developers to create User-Defined Functions (UDFs) for custom operations. 1. Types of Functions: • Built-in Functions: o Provided by Pig for common tasks such as string manipulation, mathematical calculations, type conversions, and date processing. o Examples: ▪ Mathematical: ABS(), CEIL(), FLOOR(), ROUND() ▪ String: CONCAT(), SUBSTRING(), TRIM(), UPPER(), LOWER() ▪ Date/Time: CURRENT_TIME(), ToDate() ▪ Aggregation: SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MAX(), MIN() • User-Defined Functions (UDFs): o Custom functions implemented to handle complex logic or special processing not covered by built-in functions. o Can be Filter UDFs, Eval UDFs, Load UDFs, or Store UDFs. 2. Usage of Functions: • Functions are applied within Pig Latin statements, usually inside FOREACH...GENERATE or FILTER commands. • Example: B = FOREACH A GENERATE UPPER(name), age + 5;

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 16 C = FILTER A BY age > 18 AND LOWER(city) == 'delhi'; • Functions can also be nested or combined to create complex expressions. 3. Parameters: • Functions can accept constants, field values, or expressions as parameters. • They return a value of a specific type depending on the function's operation. 4. Advantages of Functions: • Simplify complex transformations by encapsulating operations. • Enhance code readability and maintainability. • Reduce repetitive logic across scripts. • Facilitate modular design when combined with UDFs and macros. 5. Best Practices: • Prefer built-in functions for efficiency unless custom logic is necessary. • Keep expressions clear and avoid overly complex nested functions. • Use UDFs for reusable or highly specialized logic. • Document the purpose and behavior of custom functions to ensure maintainability. Functions in Pig are essential for effective data processing, allowing both built -in operations and custom logic to transform, analyze, and compute large -scale datasets efficiently.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 17 7. Macros Macros in Pig - Detailed Explanation Macros in Pig Latin are reusable blocks of Pig Latin code that allow developers to encapsulate frequently used operations, reducing redundancy and simplifying script maintenance. Macros are similar to functions in traditional programming languages but are specific to Pig Latin scripts. Key Points About Macros: 1. Purpose of Macros: o Promote code reusability by encapsulating repetitive Pig Latin code. o Simplify complex scripts by breaking them into smaller, manageable parts. o Make scripts more readable and maintainable. 2. Defining Macros: o Macros are defined using the DEFINE keyword or MACRO keyword followed by a name and parameters. o Syntax: DEFINE macro_name(parameter1, parameter2, ...) { -- Pig Latin statements } o Example: DEFINE filterAdults(relation) { filtered = FILTER relation BY age >= 18; GENERATE filtered;

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 18 } 3. Calling Macros: o Once defined, a macro can be called by passing the required parameters. o Example: adultUsers = filterAdults(users); 4. Parameters: o Macros can accept multiple parameters, including relations, constants, or expressions. o This makes them versatile for various operations and datasets. 5. Scope and Reusability: o Macros exist within the Pig script and can be reused multiple times in the same script. o They can also be stored in external Pig script files and included using the IMPORT statement for reuse across scripts. 6. Advantages of Macros: o Reduces Code Duplication: Encapsulates repetitive logic. o Improves Maintainability: Changes in macro logic automatically apply wherever the macro is used. o Enhances Readability: Breaks complex scripts into logical, understandable components. o Parameterization: Allows dynamic behavior based on input parameters. 7. Best Practices: o Keep macros focused on a single logical task. o Name macros descriptively to indicate their functionality. o Avoid heavy computation inside macros; delegate such tasks to UDFs if needed. o Document macros clearly for maintainability and team collaboration. Macros, along with UDFs, provide Pig Latin with modularity and reusability, making large-scale data processing more efficient, maintainable, and organized.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 19 The section on Macros in Pig has been expanded into a detailed explanation, covering definition, parameters, usage, advantages, scope, and best practices for clar ity and comprehensive understanding. 8. User-Defined Functions (UDFs) User-Defined Functions (UDFs) in Pig - Detailed Explanation User-Defined Functions (UDFs) in Pig allow developers to extend Pig Latin's built -in functionality by implementing custom processing logic. UDFs are particularly useful when the standard operators and functions do not meet the specific needs of a data processing task. Key Points About UDFs: 1. Purpose of UDFs: o Perform operations that cannot be achieved with Pig's built-in functions. o Handle complex transformations, aggregations, or data filtering. o Enable code reuse and modularization in Pig scripts. 2. Types of UDFs: o Filter UDF: ▪ Used to filter tuples based on custom conditions. ▪ Example: Remove records with invalid email addresses. ▪ Syntax: REGISTER 'myFilterUDF.jar'; B = FILTER A BY myFilterUDF(field); A. Filter UDF – Purpose: Filter data using custom logic. Java Example: public class AgeFilter extends FilterFunc { public Boolean exec(Tuple input) throws IOException { int age = (Integer) input.get(0);

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 20 return age > 18; } } o Eval UDF: ▪ Evaluates input values and returns a new value or transformed output. ▪ Example: Convert all string names to uppercase. ▪ Syntax: REGISTER 'myEvalUDF.jar'; B = FOREACH A GENERATE myEvalUDF(name); B. Eval UDF – Purpose: Return transformed data. Java Example: public class ToUpper extends EvalFunc<String> { public String exec(Tuple input) throws IOException { return input.get(0).toString().toUpperCase(); } } o Load UDF: ▪ Custom functions for loading data from non-standard sources. ▪ Example: Load JSON data or XML files. ▪ Syntax: REGISTER 'myLoadUDF.jar'; A = LOAD 'data.json' USING myLoadUDF(); Load UDF – Purpose: Custom way of reading data from a source (e.g., JSON). o Store UDF: ▪ Custom functions to store data into specialized formats or locations. ▪ Example: Save output in a specific compressed format or database.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 21 3. Implementation: o UDFs are typically written in Java, though Pig also supports Python, JavaScript, and other scripting languages via Pig Streaming. o The UDF class must extend one of Pig's abstract UDF classes such as EvalFunc, FilterFunc, LoadFunc, or StoreFunc. 4. Registration and Usage: o UDFs must be compiled into a JAR file and registered in the Pig script using the REGISTER command. o Once registered, UDFs can be called within Pig Latin statements just like built-in functions. 5. Advantages of UDFs: o Flexibility to implement complex logic. o Reusability across multiple Pig scripts. o Maintainable and modular code. o Integration with custom data sources or output formats. 6. Best Practices: o Keep UDFs simple and focused on a single task. o Avoid heavy computation inside UDFs to prevent performance bottlenecks. o Write unit tests for UDFs to ensure correctness. o Document UDF behavior for better maintainability. UDFs significantly enhance Pig’s power, making it possible to handle specialized processing requirements and complex data transformations that are not feasible with built-in operators alone ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 22 1. Data Flow: o Pig Latin scripts represent a logical sequence of operations. o Intermediate results are stored in relations, which are passed to subsequent operations. o Enables modular and step-by-step transformation of data. 2. Comments: o Single-line comments: -- This is a comment o Multi-line comments: /* Comment block */ o Useful for documenting complex scripts. 3. Modularity and Reusability: o Pig Latin supports macros and UDFs for reusable code blocks and custom functions. o Encourages clean, maintainable scripts that can handle large -scale data efficiently. This detailed structure helps developers fully leverage Pig Latin for scalable, flexible, and efficient data processing on Hadoop.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 23 Flume: working with flume, Transactions and Reliability, The HDFS Sink, Fan Out, Distribution Apache Flume is a distributed, reliable, and available service designed for efficiently collecting, aggregating, and moving large amounts of log data from various sources to centralized storage such as HDFS or HBase. It is commonly used for streaming data ingestion in Hadoop ecosystems. 1. Purpose of Flume: • Collects data from multiple sources, including application logs, social media feeds, and event data. • Aggregates and transports data to centralized storage for processing and analysis. • Ensures reliability and fault tolerance in data flow. 2. Core Components: • Event: The basic unit of data in Flume, usually a single log entry or message. • Source: Component that receives data from external sources and converts it into

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 24 Flume events. o Examples: Avro Source, Thrift Source, Syslog Source. • Channel: Temporary storage between source and sink. o Types: Memory Channel, File Channel, JDBC Channel. • Sink: Component that delivers events to the final destination. o Examples: HDFS Sink, HBase Sink, Logger Sink. 3. Flume Architecture: • Flume follows a simple and flexible architecture: Source → Channel → Sink. • Supports multi-hop flows, where events can pass through multiple Flume agents before reaching the destination. • Ensures reliability using transactional guarantees between source, channel, and sink. 4. Reliability and Fault Tolerance: • Flume provides transactional channels to prevent data loss. • Channels store events until the sink successfully writes them to the destination. • In case of failure, Flume agents retry delivery automatically. 5. Scalability: • Flume agents can be scaled horizontally to handle high-volume data streams. • Supports load balancing and failover to maintain uninterrupted data flow. 6. Data Flow Configuration: • Flume is configured using simple configuration files specifying sources, channels, and sinks. • Example: agent1.sources = src1

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 25 agent1.sinks = sink1 agent1.channels = ch1 agent1.sources.src1.type = exec agent1.sources.src1.command = tail -F /var/log/syslog agent1.sinks.sink1.type = hdfs agent1.sinks.sink1.hdfs.path = hdfs://namenode/flume/logs/%Y/%m/%d/%H/ agent1.channels.ch1.type = memory agent1.sources.src1.channels = ch1 agent1.sinks.sink1.channel = ch1 Flume in Hadoop This section covers Flume's working, transactions and reliability, HDFS sink, fan-out, and data distribution mechanisms in detail. 1. Working with Flume: • Flume collects, aggregates, and transports large volumes of event data from sources to storage systems. • Data Flow: Events are generated at the source → stored temporarily in a channel → delivered to a sink. • Agents: Flume runs as an agent on each host; each agent contains a source, channel, and sink.

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 26 • Multi-hop architecture allows events to pass through several agents before reaching the final sink. • Supports dynamic configuration, allowing agents to be added or removed without downtime. 2. Transactions and Reliability: • Flume ensures reliable delivery through transactional semantics between source, channel, and sink. • Transaction Lifecycle: 1. Source starts a transaction and writes events to the channel. 2. Channel stores events and commits the transaction if successful. 3. Sink reads events from the channel and writes them to the destination. 4. Transactions are rolled back on failure to prevent data loss. • Channel Types: o Memory Channel: Fast but volatile. o File Channel: Durable, writes events to disk for fault tolerance. • Retries and failover mechanisms ensure uninterrupted event delivery. 3. The HDFS Sink: • A Flume sink that writes collected events directly to HDFS. • Supports configurable file roll policies: by size, time, or number of events. • Ensures atomic writes and fault tolerance using transactions. • Example configuration: agent1.sinks.hdfsSink.type = hdfs agent1.sinks.hdfsSink.hdfs.path = hdfs://namenode/flume/events/%Y/%m/%d/%H/ agent1.sinks.hdfsSink.hdfs.fileType = DataStream agent1.sinks.hdfsSink.hdfs.rollInterval = 60

Prepared by K.Chandram Assistant Professor Anurag University Page 27 agent1.sinks.hdfsSink.channel = ch1 4. Fan-Out in Flume: • Fan-Out allows one source to send the same event to multiple sinks simultaneously. • Useful when multiple storage systems need to receive the same data. • Achieved using a channel per sink and configuring each sink to subscribe to the source's output. 5. Data Distribution: • Flume supports distributing events across multiple sinks for load balancing and fault tolerance. • Ensures high throughput and avoids bottlenecks. • Can implement multiplexing to route events based on content, such as sending logs from different servers to different directories in HDFS. • Enables scalable and reliable ingestion of streaming data into Hadoop ecosystems. Best Practices: • Use file channels for high reliability in production environments. • Optimize fan-out and distribution configurations for throughput and fault tolerance. • Monitor agent health and channel status to prevent bottlenecks. • Configure HDFS sinks with appropriate roll policies to balance write performance and file management. By understanding these advanced aspect s, Flume can be effectively leveraged for real - time, reliable, and scalable data ingestion into Hadoop.
NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING
UNIT-2 LEXICAL SEMANTICS

linguistic study of word meaning is called lexical semantics sing is the lemma for sing, sang, sung. In many languages the infinitive form is used as the lemma for the verb, so Spanish dormir “to sleep” is the lemma for duermes “you sleep”. The specific forms sung or carpets or sing or duermes are called wordforms. As the example above shows, each lemma can have multiple meanings; the lemma mouse can refer to the rodent or the cursor control device. We call each of these aspects of the meaning of mouse a word sense.

Synonymy One important component of word meaning is the relationship between word senses.  For example when one word has a sense whose meaning is identical to a sense of another word, or nearly identical, we say the two senses of those two words are synonyms. Synonyms include such pairs as  couch/sofa vomit/throw up filbert/hazelnut car/automobile propositional meaning- two words have the same meaning which doesn’t change the truth of sentence.
Word similarity Word Relatedness The meaning of two words can be related in ways other than similarity. Ex:coffee and cup are clearly related

A semantic field is a set of words which cover a particular semantic domain and bear structured relations with each other. For example, words might be related by being in the semantic field of hospitals (surgeon, scalpel, nurse, anesthetic, hospital), restaurants (waiter, menu, plate, food, chef)
words have affective meanings or connotations- Positive connotations –happy, negative connotations-sad Positive or negative evaluation language is called sentiment
3 dimensions of a word in vector.

Vector Semantics Vector semantics is the standard way to represent word meaning in NLP , helping us model many of the aspects of word meaning we saw in the previous section. The idea of vector semantics is to represent a word as a point in a multidimensional semantic space that is derived from the distributions of word neighbors. Vectors for representing words are called embeddings .
Words and Vectors In a term-document matrix, each row represents a word in the vocabulary and each column represents a document from some collection of documents.

A vector space is a collection of vectors, characterized by their dimension. In the example in Fig. 6.3, the document vectors are of dimension 4, just so they fit on the page; in real term-document matrices, the vectors representing each document would have dimensionality |V|, the vocabulary size.

Words as vectors: document dimensions vector semantics can also be used to represent the meaning of words, by associating each word with a word vector. a row vector rather than a column vector, hence with different dimensions, as shown in Fig. 6.5. The four dimensions of the vector for fool, [36,58,1,4], correspond to the four Shakespeare plays. Word counts in the same four dimensions are used to form the vectors for the other 3 words: wit, [20,15,2,3]; battle, [1,0,7,13]; and good [114,80,62,89].

An alternative to using the term-document matrix to represent words as vectors of document counts, is to use the term-term matrix, also called the word-word matrix or the term-context matrix. This matrix is thus of dimensionality |V|×|V| and each cell records the number of times the row (target) word and the column (context) word co- occur in some context in some training corpus. The context could be the document, in which case the cell represents the number of times the two words appear in the same document. It is most common, however, to use smaller contexts. for example of 4 words to the left and 4 words to the right, in which case the cell represents the number of times (in some training corpus) the column word occurs in such a ±4 word window around the row word.
If we then take every occurrence of each word (say strawberry) and count the context words around it, we get a word-word co- occurrence matrix.
Cosine for measuring similarity To measure similarity between two target words v and w,the most common similarity metric is the cosine of the angle between the vectors.

Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI)

The numerator tells us how often we observed the two words together (assuming we compute probability by using the MLE). The denominator tells us how often we would expect the two words to co-occur assuming they each occurred independently; recall that the probability of two independent events both occurring is just the product of the probabilities of the two events. Thus, the ratio gives us an estimate of how much more the two words co-occur than we expect by chance. PMI is a useful tool whenever we need to find words that are strongly associated
PMI values range from negative to positive infinity. For this reason it is more common to use Positive PMI (called PPMI) which replaces all negative PMI values with zero.
